activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: The Japanese word origami comes from 'ori', meaning to fold, and 'kami', meaning paper.
story:
Kaitlyn flattened the last fold of her paper crane and set it on the library table, next to Remi's lopsided frog and Veronica's perfect star. The crane looked wrong, like a bird that had given up halfway through flying. "Mine keeps coming out sinister," she said, tilting her head at it. "Like it's plotting something."

"That's because you're folding the wings too early," Veronica said, not looking up from her star.

"You fold when the diagram says fold," Remi argued. "The diagram is the boss."

Kaitlyn remembered the first club meeting, three weeks ago, when Ms. Halvorsen had put a stack of square paper in the middle of the table and said she would be around if anyone needed her, but mostly they could figure things out themselves. Remi had taught Veronica the waterbomb base that day, and Veronica had let Remi borrow the good scissors. They had figured out they cooperated better than they competed. But today nobody could agree on anything, and Kaitlyn's crane had gone from hopeful to hunched.

The real argument had started when Remi claimed the club should be called something else. "Origami isn't even about paper," he insisted. "It just means folding. Like, folding in general."

"It means paper too," Veronica said. "My grandmother told me. The word comes from 'ori', meaning to fold, and 'kami', meaning paper."

Remi rolled his eyes. "Prove it."

Kaitlyn slid her chair back and marched to the nonfiction shelves, where she'd seen a book about Japan during her last visit. She found it, flipped through the glossy pages, and there it was, in a caption beside a photo of a thousand paper cranes strung on thread. Ori, to fold. Kami, paper. She carried the book back like evidence and set it open in front of Remi. He read it twice, his ears going pink.

"Fine," he said. "The diagram is still the boss, though."

"Then let's follow it together," Kaitlyn said. "Read it out, one step at a time, and I'll fold while you two watch for where I go wrong."

Remi read. Veronica pointed out the exact fold where Kaitlyn's wings had gone crooked, the third one, where the paper had to be turned over first. Kaitlyn started again with a fresh square, feeling the creases stiffen under her thumbnail, hearing the soft crackle each time the paper gave in.

The second crane stood up straight, wings even, beak pointed at the window. Kaitlyn turned it toward Remi. "Say it's not plotting something."

Remi laughed so loud that Ms. Halvorsen glanced over from the front desk and raised one finger to her lips.

activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
knowledge_domain: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
fact: The cast shadow is the shadow the sphere throws onto the surface it rests on, and it always falls on the side opposite the light source.
story:
Lily set her sketchbook on the picnic table under the pine canopy and squinted at the golf ball Mr. Rao had given each camper. "Watch," she said to Flynn. "He wants a sphere with a highlight, a shadow, and the shadow it throws on the table." She tapped her pencil. "But he won't tell us where the thrown one goes. He said we have to figure it out ourselves."

"That's so unfair," Flynn said, grinning anyway. "But fun." They sat by the mess hall window, where afternoon sun poured in from the left. Lily shaded a bright spot on her ball where the light hit it, then a dark crescent on the far side. So far so good. Then, feeling clever, she drew a long stretched oval sliding off the left side of the sphere, away from the light. She held it up. "Done!"

Flynn leaned over and burst out laughing. "Lily, look at your real ball." On the table, the actual golf ball sat in bright sunshine, and its shadow lay dark and solid on the right, the side far from the window. Lily flipped her sketch around, then looked again at the ball, then back at her drawing. "I put it backwards," she said. "The shadow it throws goes on the side opposite the light. Every time." Her pencil was already moving, erasing the wrong oval and redrawing it on the right, squashed against the imaginary tabletop.

"Quick, test it again before class," Flynn said, and they ran the ball to the other window, where the light came from the right. The shadow had scooted to the left. Lily whooped so loudly that Rosie looked up from her bracelet and came jogging over, agile across the tree roots. "What are you two collaborating on?" she asked, and Lily showed her the page: highlight, shadow, cast shadow, all in the right places.

When Mr. Rao walked by, Lily turned her sketchbook toward him. He studied it, then raised an eyebrow at the ball by the window. "Well," he said. "Someone's been observing." Lily slid her pencil behind her ear and said, "Same side as the dark part of the ball. Opposite the light. Try me."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Delayed muscle soreness is not caused by lactic acid, which returns to normal levels within about an hour after exercise.
story:
Rachel's whole body ached, and it had only started hurting the morning after Saturday's soccer game. She lay in the grass of her backyard while Andreanne juggled the ball and Nikolai collapsed beside her, groaning.

"It's the lactic acid," Nikolai said. "My cousin told me. It builds up during a game and then it attacks your muscles the next day."

Rachel frowned at the sky. That didn't fit. She'd once twisted her ankle at practice, and Mr. Huang, whose yard backed onto hers, had been reading a physiology book on his porch at the time. He'd mentioned something offhand, and she'd looked it up afterward because she was curious. "Lactic acid goes back to normal within about an hour after exercise," she said. "It's gone long before the next morning even starts."

"Then why are we sore?" Nikolai asked.

Rachel sat up, an idea forming. "If it isn't that, then something else is doing it. So it's something slow." She thought about the tomato plants Mr. Huang had shown her last spring, how a hornworm larva could chew a leaf all night and you'd only find the damage in the morning. Invisible cause, delayed effect. "Maybe exercise leaves behind something that takes a whole day to show up," she said. "Like the way we couldn't figure out what was eating his tomatoes until we found that fat green larva."

"So my cousin just made it up?" Nikolai said.

"Or he's repeating something people used to believe," Andreanne said, trapping the ball under her foot. "Face it, you're gullible. You believed the thing about gum staying in your stomach for seven years too."

Nikolai was quiet for a moment. "Okay," he said. "Then it's not lactic acid. But it's still something, and it still hurts, so can somebody please help me stand up?"

Rachel grabbed his hand and pulled. Behind them, Mr. Huang's porch light flicked on and began to emit its pale evening glow over the fence.

"Practice again tomorrow," Andreanne said. "We'll test if it gets worse."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: The bandwagon technique urges people to do or buy something because "everyone else is," appealing to the wish to belong rather than giving a reason.
story:
The whole sixth grade revolved around the fall fundraiser, because the class trip to the science center would only happen if they sold enough reusable water bottles. Matteo wanted the trip so badly he could taste it, so he volunteered to make the poster. He printed his slogan in huge letters: "Join the millions who already switched!" and taped it above the cafeteria cash table.

At lunch, Mathieu squinted at it. "Switched from what? Millions of who?" He picked up one of the bottles and turned it over. "Does it keep water cold longer, or what?"

"It says millions," Matteo said. "That's the point."

"That's not a reason, though. That's just everybody doing it." Vada, who was stacking bottles to help, tapped the poster. "My brother calls that the bandwagon technique. It makes you want to belong instead of telling you why the thing is good."

Matteo felt his ears go warm. He tested a simple idea: he made a second poster that read "Keeps your water cold for hours, and every bottle sends our class to the science center," and hung it in the gym hallway where the same number of kids walked by each day. All week he counted sales, keeping tallies proportional to foot traffic, since the gym hallway got more people than the cafeteria.

On Friday the numbers didn't lie. The gym poster had sold nearly twice as many bottles. Mr. Huang stopped by the table, bought one, and looked at both posters for a long moment. "Interesting experiment," he said, and Matteo changed the cafeteria poster on the spot, peeling off his old slogan. Mathieu came back with three quarters, held one up, and asked, "So does it actually keep water cold?" Matteo filled a bottle from the fountain, handed it over, and said, "Try it and see."

activity: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
knowledge_domain: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
fact: Hormones during puberty make the skin's oil glands produce more oil, called sebum, which can clog pores and cause acne.
story:
Benjamin found the pimple on Tuesday night, right under the brim of his nose, and camp photos were scheduled for Thursday morning. He pressed it, made it worse, and then leaned close to the mirror in the washhouse while mosquitoes whined against the screen. Wilder came in behind him, lugging a towel and a bottle of shampoo.

"Is that a zit?" Wilder asked. "My brother had them all over his forehead last year."

"It wasn't there this morning," Benjamin said. "So something happened between breakfast and lights-out. Something I can't see." He had skipped his shower after the swamp hike, and again after capture the flag. He'd also let Wilder talk him into a second helping of the greasy foil-pack dinners, but the pimple had shown up under his nose, not on his chin, and he wanted to be fair about the evidence.

"Here's my idea," he told Wilder. "I shower every single time I sweat between now and photos. Tonight, before breakfast, before the morning activity. If sweat or dirt is causing it, new ones shouldn't show up." Wilder agreed to accompany him to the washhouse each time, mostly because he liked sneaking past the counselors' cabin with a flashlight.

On Wednesday morning they cornered Charlee at the craft table, where she was bending a wire star for the friendship bracelets. She was the only one at camp who read her mom's medical books for fun. "It's called sebum," she said, not looking up from the wire. "Oil. During puberty your hormones make your skin's oil glands pump out more of it, and it clogs your pores. That's the pimple." Benjamin stared at his reflection in the polished alloy lid of the craft bin. So washing mattered, but scrubbing his face raw wouldn't shut down the oil. It was underneath, working whether he watched or not.

He still showered three more times that day, used the deodorant Mr. Van Dijk handed out at the supply shed without a word, and slept with his elastic swim cap pulled over his forehead as an experiment he'd rather not explain. On Thursday he stood in line behind Wilder, chin up. The photographer counted down, the flash went off, and Benjamin smiled with his whole face, pimple and all.

activity: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score
knowledge_domain: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score
fact: Ticking the checkbox beside a Scratch variable shows a monitor on the stage, so players can watch the score change.
story:
Grandpa's house smelled like sawdust because the workers were there to renovate the kitchen, so Felix had set up his laptop on the ping-pong table in the basement, the only room where nobody was hammering anything. He had until three o'clock to finish his cat-and-cheese game, because Mackenzie was coming over to test it before they both had to submit their projects for computer club on Monday.

Mackenzie arrived early, which was typical. She grabbed the trackpad, moved the cat with the arrow keys, touched the cheese, and heard the little blip that Felix had recorded of himself going "wahoo." She did it again. Wahoo. Then she frowned.

"Okay, I touched it twice. What's my score?"

"Two, obviously. The variable goes up by one every time."

"It says nothing on the stage. There's no score anywhere. For all I know the wahoos are decorative." She touched the cheese five more times, rapidly, like she was proving a point.

Felix leaned over his own program, feeling defensive. The variable was right there in the block, Score change by 1, wrapped inside a loop, guarded by an if-then block that checked whether the cat was touching the cheese. He had reasoned it all out carefully. But Mackenzie was right that the stage showed nothing, which meant the game was, in the most probable sense of the word, broken. He clicked the checkbox beside the variable, just to see what it did, and a small number appeared in the corner of the stage.

"Oh," said Mackenzie. "Tick the box beside the variable and it shows up. That's the monitor. Everyone can watch it change." She reset the score to zero and started a real run.

"Grandpa," Felix called up the stairs later, "did you know the checkbox makes a monitor?"

Grandpa, who had spent the morning arguing with the workers about tile, called back down, "I still don't know how the microwave clock works, Felix."

Mackenzie set a new high score of seventeen, then a better one of twenty-one. Felix had planned to keep the score hidden for mystery, but watching the number climb turned out to be the best part, so he typed his grandpa's new neighbours, the refugee family from the flat upstairs, into the credits as beta testers, which was only half true. He ran upstairs anyway, laptop open, score showing, and rang their doorbell.

activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
knowledge_domain: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
fact: If milk costs 2.65 and you pay with 5.00, the correct change is 2.35, whatever the currency.
story:
The permission slip said the fifth graders would walk, in pairs, from the school to the corner store and back with one small errand each. Ella read it three times at her desk while Ms. Moretti wrote the practice problem on the board: milk costs 2.65, you pay with 5.00, what is your change? Across the room, Kaelyn was already scribbling. "It's 2.35," Kaelyn whispered, sliding her paper diagonally across the aisle so Ella could see. "Count up from 2.65. Thirty-five cents gets you to three dollars, then two more dollars gets you to five." Ella copied the number into her own notebook and counted it twice more on her fingers, because tomorrow the money would be real.

At lunch, Makenna declared herself the veteran of the trip, since she had walked to that store with her older sister at least ten times. "The cashier never counts your change for you," Makenna said. "You have to do it yourself, fast, right there at the counter. You can't stand there like a fence post." Ella practiced with play coins from the math bin until the bell rang, paying an imaginary 5.00 over and over and checking for 2.35.

The next afternoon, Ms. Moretti transmitted the class envelope of errands at the door, one task per pair, and Ella and Kaelyn drew milk. The walk took six minutes. The store smelled like oranges and floor cleaner. Ella found the small carton, carried it to the counter, and handed over her five-dollar bill, feeling her heart tap like a knuckle on a door.

The cashier rang it up, dropped coins into Ella's palm, and turned to the next customer. Ella looked down. Two quarters, no, she counted by touching each coin, one, two, three. "Wait," she said, and her voice came out smaller than she wanted. She counted again anyway. "I only got 2.15." She pointed at the register screen, which said 2.65. "The milk is 2.65 and I paid 5.00, so the change is 2.35. That's thirty-five cents plus two dollars. You gave me two dollars and fifteen cents."

The cashier looked at the screen, then at the drawer, and shook his head at himself. "You're right, I missed a coin." He set two dimes on the counter. Ella picked them up and counted the whole pile one last time: two dollars, thirty-five cents, exactly. Kaelyn, waiting by the door with the milk, held up both thumbs.

On the walk back, Kaelyn said, "You didn't stand there like a fence post." Ella jingled the coins in her pocket. "Next time," she said, "I'm counting before he even closes the drawer."

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: In 1668 Francesco Redi put meat in jars; maggots grew in open jars, but not in jars covered with gauze that kept flies off the meat.
story:
Chloe set a sealed bag of old bananas on the lab table. "Leo says rotten fruit makes fruit flies all by itself," she told Ms. Huang. "He says you can leave a peach in a jar for a week and the flies just appear out of it. I think they come from outside. He won a dollar off Alena betting on it, and now he wants my dollar too."

Ms. Huang looked at the bananas, then opened a cabinet and took out two wide glass jars, a square of gauze, and a rubber band. "In 1668, a man named Francesco Redi did something a lot like what you want to do," she said. "He put meat in jars." She handed Chloe the jars. "Want to invest your dollar in an experiment instead of a bet?"

Chloe and Alena cut two equal chunks of banana and dropped one into each jar. They left the first jar open on the windowsill. Over the second jar they stretched the gauze and snapped the elastic band around the rim, so the top was covered but air could still get in. Alena wrote both jars' locations on a strip of tape. "If flies show up in the open one and not in the covered one," Chloe said, "then the flies aren't coming out of the fruit."

"Fine, but if flies show up in both, I keep the dollar," said a voice from the next table. Leo had drifted over with his notebook. "And if neither jar gets flies, that means your bananas are just lame." He tapped the covered jar with his pencil. "What's the gauze even for? It's not a lid."

"It keeps flies off the banana," Alena said. Ms. Huang was across the room helping another group, so nobody explained anything further. Chloe wrote her guess at the top of her lab sheet: flies will grow in the open jar, and not in the covered jar. Under "hypothesis," she copied it in smaller letters, because a guess you can test deserved its official name.

For three days nothing happened. On the fourth day Leo crowed, and Chloe refused to look until fifth period, when she made herself walk to the windowsill. In the open jar, two small flies crawled over the banana chunk and one bumped against the glass. She leaned close to the covered jar. The banana inside had gone brown and soft, and there was not a single fly, egg, or speck of maggot anywhere on it or on the gauze.

"It's a testable guess," Chloe said to Leo, holding up her lab sheet. "The experiment supported mine and overturned yours. A dollar." Leo dug in his pocket, but instead of handing the bill over, he slapped it on the table and picked up the covered jar, squinting through the gauze at the flyless banana. "Okay," he said. "But next time we're doing it with the fruit flies that live in my mom's compost, because I still think her compost is basically agriculture." Alena snorted, and Chloe slid the dollar off the table and into her back pocket.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Feeling anxious sometimes is normal, but when anxiety is intense, lasts a long time and gets in the way of daily life, a doctor may diagnose an anxiety disorder, which is treatable.
story:
At nine on Tuesday night, Payton's phone buzzed again. The group chat, which Mr. Martínez had set up for the science fair team, was supposed to be about their volcano project, but Landyn had written seventeen messages in a row, each one faster than the last. "What if the baking soda doesn't work. What if Damon drops the tray. What if we get up there and I forget everything." Damon replied with three eye-roll emojis and the words "calm down," which made Landyn type even faster. Payton put her chin in her hands. This wasn't Landyn's usual worrying about a forgotten homework sheet. It had been going on for two weeks, since before the project even started, and it wasn't stopping.

She tried something. Instead of telling Landyn to relax, which clearly backfired, she wrote, "Damon, she's not wrong that carrying the tray is a big job. Landyn, you hold the bottle, I'll do the talking part, Damon carries. Deal?" Damon typed "fine," and Landyn typed "ok." It felt like mediating a treaty between her two older cousins at Thanksgiving, but smaller. Then, before anyone could restart the argument, Payton added, "Also, phone down at ten. Mr. Martínez said chat is for project stuff only, and I'm setting that boundary for me too. My mom keeps checking her news app and talking about a recession and it stresses me out, and staring at screens doesn't help." She silenced her phone and actually went to sleep.

Wednesday at lunch, Landyn sat down across from her, tray wobbling slightly. "Can I tell you something?" She kept her voice low, glancing at the table behind them. "It's not just the volcano. I couldn't sleep all week. My mom took me to the doctor yesterday." She stabbed her fork at nothing. "The doctor said feeling anxious sometimes is normal, but when it's really strong, and it lasts a long time, and it gets in the way of stuff like school and sleeping, it can be an anxiety disorder. That's what I have. And it's treatable, so I'm going to start getting help for it."

Payton slid her chocolate milk across the table. "Is that why 'calm down' never worked?" Landyn almost smiled. "Yeah. It's like telling a sneeze to stop." Damon dropped onto the bench with his own tray, having apparently heard everything, and pointed his fork at the two of them. "So I'll carry the tray, and I'll stop saying that." Payton stacked her napkin under the wobbly leg of the table and said, "I'm feeling optimistic about Friday." Landyn took a long drink of the milk and set it down. "Me too," she said. "A little, anyway."

activity: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score
knowledge_domain: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score
fact: In Scratch, a 'repeat 10' block runs the blocks inside it exactly ten times, while a 'forever' block keeps going until the program is stopped.
story:
Hailey slid into the seat beside Kesler at the library computers, tablet already warm under her arm. The Scratch club met every Saturday in the corner by the windows, and today was the day her game would finally work. Her monster was supposed to chase the player's cat across the screen, and every touch was supposed to cost a point. The score, though, kept doing something strange.

"Watch," she said. She pressed the green flag. The monster stomped across the stage, then stopped dead in the middle like it had fallen asleep.

"You used repeat ten," Ludovic said, leaning over from the next computer. "Repeat ten runs whatever's inside it exactly ten times. Ten steps, then it's finished. Nothing else happens unless you tell it to."

Hailey stared at her stack of blocks. Ten. She counted the stomps on screen to be sure, and there they were, exactly ten, then freeze. She had assumed the monster would just keep going, but the block was doing precisely what it said, nothing more. Her problem wasn't mysterious at all. It was sitting right there, shaped like an orange loop.

"So what if I want him to chase me the whole game?" she asked.

"You want forever," Ludovic said. "Forever keeps going until you stop the program."

Ms. Esposito, who ran the club, paused at their table on her slow circuit around the room. Hailey held up the screen before she could circulate past. "Look, my monster moves now!" She had swapped the repeat block for the forever block, and the monster lunged after the cat, over and over, while her if-then block ticked the score down each time it got close.

"My if-then was working the whole time," Hailey said, grinning at Kesler. "The monster just never reached the cat after step ten." The concept had seemed so ambiguous that morning, and now it felt obvious. "One more touch and I lose. Try to beat me."

Kesler grabbed the mouse. "Green flag. Go."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Gleaning means gathering crops left in fields after harvest, and some groups send volunteers to glean farms so the produce can go to food banks.
story:
Cooper read the note taped to the food bank's back door twice before pushing it open. "Cooper, the Saturday crew is short. Ride with Henri and Celine to Miller's farm. Bring gloves. Mr. Dang." Inside, the sorting room smelled like cardboard and apples, and Celine was already loading crates into a van.

"I thought we'd be stacking cans," Cooper said, climbing in beside Henri.

"Farms first," Henri said. "You'll see."

The farmer met them at the edge of a brown field, its potato plants already cut and gone. Behind him, the ground was littered with pale lumps half buried in the dirt. Cooper frowned. The harvest was over, so why were they here? Then he noticed the pattern: the machine that dug the potatoes had clearly missed rows, leaving a whole crop behind, wasted unless somebody came for it. The farmer wanted it gathered, and the food bank wanted potatoes, so this was the missing link between them.

"Gleaning," Celine said, pulling on her gloves. "That's what this is called. Gathering crops left in fields after harvest. Some groups send volunteers out to glean farms so the produce can go to food banks."

They set to work. Cooper filled his first crate slowly, then figured out a rhythm, kneeling and scooping along the missed rows, and by noon he felt almost competent at spotting the buried ones by the tiny cracks they left in the soil. Mr. Dang arrived with sandwiches and a clipboard to coordinate the pickups, telling each driver which food bank would take how many crates. Cooper ate his sandwich in the warm dirt smell of the field, dirt under his fingernails, sun on his neck.

"Eight hundred pounds," Mr. Dang announced at the end of the day, tallying the crates. Then he grinned and held up a potato the size of a softball. "The farmer says it's the biggest one ever left in this field, and it's yours, Cooper. You found it."

Cooper turned the ugly, wonderful thing over in his muddy hands. "Dinner," he said, and Celine laughed all the way back to the van.

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
knowledge_domain: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
fact: Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria break down dead plants and animals, returning nutrients to the soil that producers use again.
story:
Zack stared at the blank poster paper and wished the hawk would appear and draw itself. Ms. Holloway had said the whole class had to make a food chain starting with the sun and ending with a top predator, and then explain what happened if one link disappeared. His chain was easy enough. Sun, grass, rabbit, hawk. He had drawn the hawk four times already, and every time its talons looked like carrots.

Reuben leaned over from the next desk. "You're still on the sun? I'm on my third predator."

"Your fox looks like a dog," Zack said, but without much force. The real problem wasn't the drawing. It was the second question, the one about a link disappearing. He kept thinking about last summer at his grandmother's garden, when he had found a fat brown log half buried under the tomato plants, covered in pale mushrooms. He had asked his grandfather what the mushrooms were doing there, and his grandfather had knelt down and poked the soft crumbling wood with one finger. "They're eating this old log," he had said. "Fungi and bacteria like these break down dead plants and animals, and the nutrients go back into the soil. The tomatoes drink them right up again." Zack had thought it was strange and a little gross. Now he wondered where mushrooms fit in his chain.

He tried squeezing them in after the hawk, but that made no sense. Mushrooms didn't hunt. He tried putting them beside the grass, but they didn't make food from sunlight either. Finally he drew a loop at the bottom of the page, an arrow from the dead rabbit and the dead hawk down to the mushrooms and bacteria, and another arrow back up to the grass. It wasn't a chain anymore. It was a chain with a door at the end that swung back to the start.

"Ms. Holloway," he said when she came by. "What happens if the decomposers disappear? Like, if you try to evade the gross part and just leave them out?"

"Try it without them," she said. "Tell me what the grass does."

Zack thought it through. The dead plants and animals would pile up, and the nutrients would stay locked inside them instead of going back into the soil. The grass would thin out. The rabbits would starve or leave, and the hawk would lose its food too. One missing loop, and the whole chain went hungry.

He picked up his pencil and started drawing the mushroom crown on his dead log, carefully this time, rounded and soft. Krish wandered over from the window and frowned at the poster. "Why is there a picture of rot in your food chain?"

"Because it's the part that keeps it running," Zack said. He traced the loop with his finger, from the hawk back down to the soil and up to the grass again. "Everything ends up there eventually. Even you, in like eighty years." Krish made a face, and Zack laughed and added one more mushroom to the log.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: Computer scientist Scott Fahlman proposed the emoticon :-) on September 19, 1982, on a Carnegie Mellon University message board, so readers could tell which posts were jokes.
story:
Maya hit send before she could second-guess herself. Her message to the class chat read, "Great, so our group project is due the same day as the science fair, perfect." Dania replied within a minute, and her words were all in capital letters: "WAIT, IT'S DUE WHEN? WHO TOLD YOU THIS?" Three more messages followed, each more panicked than the last.

Maya leaned back from the computer and stared at the screen. It had been a joke, obviously. The project was due Friday and the science fair was in April, a whole month away. She typed, "Dania, I was kidding," but that felt flat, like laughing at her own joke after nobody else had. Dania answered, "Oh. You sounded serious. You sounded like Ms. Byrne." That stung a little, because Ms. Byrne never joked about deadlines, and because Maya's dad joked about absolutely everything, as if kidding were hereditary in their family and she had inherited a double dose.

She remembered something, though, a tiny mark she had seen in an old forum screenshot. On a hunch she typed a colon, a hyphen, and a parenthesis. :-) It appeared sideways on the screen, a little smiling face, and something about it seemed to govern the whole tone of the sentence, the way a raised eyebrow does in person. She added it to her message and sent, "We have a month. :-)" Dania wrote back, "Ha! Okay. What is that little face?"

"Scott Fahlman," Maya said out loud to the empty room, reading from the website she had pulled up. "He proposed the emoticon :-) on September 19, 1982, on a Carnegie Mellon University message board, so readers could tell which posts were jokes." She copied the citation at the bottom of the page into her notes, because Ms. Byrne took off points for unsourced facts. Then she turned back to the chat, where Amaya had just posted, "Does this mean we can put little faces in our project presentation too?"

Maya grinned and typed, "Only if we also include a slide about :-)" and watched the little faces multiply down the screen.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Growth plates, areas of growing cartilage near the ends of children's bones, are weaker than the bone around them, which is why young athletes have limits on repetitive stress.
story:
Carter had been counting his own pitches all morning at the community center pitching clinic, and he knew the number before Coach said it. "That's your limit, Carter. Hand me the ball." The gym went quiet except for the squeak of sneakers. Carter stood on the rubber a second longer than he should have. Lylah, who kept the official count on her clipboard, held up her hand with all five fingers spread twice. Ten more, he thought, and he could have shown Coach what his curveball could do.

He sat on the bleachers next to Cindy, who was taping her wrist. "Why does it matter so much?" she asked. "You threw, like, a million pitches last winter." Carter shook his head. "Last winter I didn't count. That's the problem. I read there's cartilage near the ends of kids' bones, growth plates, and they're weaker than the bone around them. That's why young pitchers get pitch limits." He said it fast, the way he said things he'd just figured out. "It's not about being tired. It's about parts you can't see."

He tested the idea anyway. If repetitive stress was the hidden problem, then warm-up pitches must count as stress too, even if nobody recorded them. So he cut his warm-ups down to almost nothing and asked Lylah to count those too, just for him. She agreed, though she gave him a look. "You're trying to cheat a rule you made stricter than the coach did," she said. He was. And when he took the rubber with fresh count room, he could demonstrate exactly what he'd suspected: after the same total throws as before, his arm ached at the same point, warm-ups counted or not.

That afternoon, Ms. Nowak, who ran the center, handed him a note that had been left at the front desk, folded in half, no name on it. He opened it by the water fountain. "I pitched through my limits at this gym in eighth grade because I believed the stereotype that real athletes never stop. Now I watch from the bleachers like you. Don't be me. A kid who used to throw harder than you." Carter read it twice. The handwriting looked familiar, and then he saw it: the tall, slanted letters matched the poster in the hallway, the one of the community center's championship team. The man in the photo never missed a start, everyone said so.

Carter folded the note and put it in his pocket. Across the gym, Coach was waving him over to shag balls in the outfield, and Lylah was already jogging out with her clipboard, its transparent plastic cover catching the overhead lights. Carter ran after her. He would keep the note in his desk at home, he decided, but he wasn't sure yet whether he'd show anyone. "Hey," Lylah called, "same count tomorrow?" Carter scooped up a ball and fired it in. "Count everything."

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Leave No Trace outdoor ethics are organized as seven principles, including 'dispose of waste properly' and 'leave what you find'.
story:
The diner smelled like bacon and burnt coffee, and Aubrey slid into the booth beside her little brother, who set a fist-sized chunk of rose quartz on the table like it was a trophy. He had pried it out of a trailside wash that morning, just before they piled into the car, and he had been grinning about it ever since.

"You can't keep that," Aubrey said. "We're going back to the park tomorrow, and you have to put it back."

"Nobody will even notice," her brother said, turning the rock so the pink crystals caught the ceiling light. "It's one rock."

Aubrey remembered her class trip last spring, when Ms. Gallagher had taken them hiking and made them recite the Leave No Trace rules before they left the trailhead. She had made them count, and there were seven principles, not five and not ten. One of them was "dispose of waste properly," which was why Wren had ended up carrying her orange peel home in a plastic bag for three miles. Another one was "leave what you find," and Sofie had nearly cried when she was told she couldn't pick the little wild orchid. "Leave what you find" meant exactly what it said, even for one flower, even for one rock.

She had formulated a plan on the drive here, testing it in her head while her brother dozed against the window. If a million visitors each took one rock, she thought, the trail would slowly go bare, and nobody would be able to see the cause because each single rock looked like nothing. That was the trick of it. The evidence disappeared piece by piece.

"That rock is why the trail looks like that," she said. "Rocks hold the soil down when it rains. Take enough of them and the whole wash slides." She watched his buoyant grin fade as he looked at the quartz again, this time like it had a job to do somewhere else.

He sighed and pushed it across the table to her, and Aubrey slid it into her jacket pocket, zipping it shut. "Tomorrow, first stop," she said, and the waitress set down two plates of pancakes in front of them.

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: Hens lay eggs whether or not a rooster is present; without a rooster the eggs are unfertilized and cannot hatch into chicks.
story:
The bus rumbled up to Hartwell Living History Farm, where people in old-fashioned clothes showed how families lived a hundred and fifty years ago. Alice had helped Mr. Smith coordinate the groups that morning, taping name lists to clipboards, and she was proud to be in charge of the egg collection station.

At the henhouse, a woman in a long gray apron handed Alice a woven basket. "Six nests," she said. "Take whatever you find." Alice reached under the first hen, who squawked and shifted, and lifted out two warm brown eggs. Aditya took the next nest, and Aryanna counted the basket aloud as each egg went in.

Then Aditya frowned and looked around the yard. "There's no rooster anywhere," he said. "Does that mean these eggs could hatch if we kept them warm? Like, little chicks inside?"

Aryanna shrugged, but Alice stood still, thinking. Last summer flashed back to her: her uncle's farm, the day she'd carried a basket of eggs inside and asked her aunt the same question, and her aunt had laughed and said the hens there had no rooster either, so those eggs would never, ever be chicks. Alice hadn't believed it then. She'd even put one egg under a warm lamp for a week, turning it every day, and nothing had happened. Nothing.

"They won't hatch," Alice said now. "Hens lay eggs whether or not there's a rooster around. But without a rooster, the eggs can't turn into chicks. No rooster, no chicks. Ever."

Aditya looked relieved, in a strange way. "So these are just... breakfast."

"Exactly," Alice said.

On the way out, Aditya stopped at the electric fence by the pasture, where a yellow sign warned about high voltage. "Does it hurt a lot?" he asked, hand hovering near the wire. Aryanna, in her neutral gray jacket, nearly matched the fog behind her, and she grinned as she said, "Only one way to find out." Alice grabbed both their sleeves and pulled them toward the cider house, basket bumping against her hip, eggs safe and warm.

activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
knowledge_domain: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
fact: Slate is a metamorphic rock formed from shale, and it splits into thin flat sheets, which is why it has been used for roofs and chalkboards.
story:
The box in Grandma's cellar was supposed to hold rocks for Olivia's science project, and at first it looked like a disappointment. Inside were ten gray lumps that all seemed exactly the same, plus a note in her grandfather's handwriting: sort them properly. Her assignment was to evaluate each rock as igneous, sedimentary, or metamorphic, based on how it was formed, and identical gray lumps gave her nothing to work with. She carried the box up to the porch, where her friend Noe was waiting with the last slice of toast.

"They're all the same rock," Noe said, tipping the box side to side. "Ten copies of one boring rock. You could label the whole box and be done."

"They're not the same." Olivia held two of them together in the sunlight. One had a glittery, speckled surface, like someone had spilled sugar on it and frozen the spill. The other was smooth and layered, like pressed paper. "Speckles mean it cooled from melted stuff. That's igneous. Layers mean it settled in bits. Sedimentary." She set those two apart, which left eight smooth gray rocks with faint lines running through them.

That was when she noticed the chalkboard. It hung at the end of the porch, black and heavy, with her grandfather's old chalk still in the rail below it. Olivia had written on it a hundred times without once thinking about it, but now the lines on those eight gray rocks looked strangely familiar. She picked one up, pressed its edge against the board's surface, and felt them catch on each other, the way two pieces of the same thing do. Her heart started to pound, which felt ridiculous, but she couldn't stop it. She tapped the board with her knuckle. Cold. Solid. Not wood. Not paint over wood. She got the key from the hook by the door, unhooked the board from its nails, and turned it over. The back split away in a thin, flat sheet, and beneath it another sheet, and another, like the pages of a stone book.

"Noe," she said slowly, "the chalkboard is a rock."

Noe laughed, then stopped laughing. "Grandpa's chalkboard. The one from his school. That's a rock."

"It's the same as these." Olivia lined up one of the gray lumps beside the broken edge, and the match was exact, lines and all. She thought of the roofs in the old part of town, where the first settlement had been, all those dark squares gleaming on the wealthiest houses. Somebody had chosen this stone for the school chalkboard, and for the roofs of the affluent streets, because it split into flat sheets. She could almost hear her grandfather saying it, the way he said everything, short and sure: "Slate."

"Slate," she said out loud, testing it. "It's metamorphic, from shale."

"From shale? But shale's the layered one, the sedimentary one." Noe frowned at the smooth gray lump, then at the board, then back. "So the boring gray rocks aren't boring. They're the layered ones, changed."

Olivia looked at her three piles, then slid all eight gray rocks into the metamorphic row beside a chip of the broken board. She wrote the labels, took a photo for Mr. Menon, and then, before she could talk herself out of it, picked up the chalk and drew a line down the middle of the old slate board. On one side she wrote IGNEOUS. On the other, SEDIMENTARY. In the center, big enough to see from the yard, she wrote METAMORPHIC, UNDERSCORED IT TWICE, AND SET THE LAST GRAY ROCK ON THE CHALK RAIL, WHERE IT BELONGED.

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: Havdalah, a Hebrew word meaning separation, is the ceremony that ends Shabbat on Saturday night once three stars can be seen in the sky.
story:
Lauren's little brother thought the whole sky was against him. He had been standing at the window since dinner, pressing his nose against the glass, and now the clouds were thickening and the light was beginning to deteriorate into a gray smear.

"You promised we'd race for the stars," he said. "The whole point of tonight is the race."

"The whole point of tonight is Havdalah," Lauren said. "The race is just how we know when to start." She came and stood beside him. Her grandmother had explained it once, a long time ago, and Lauren had remembered only pieces. Something about stars. Something about the word. "Havdalah means separation," she said now, mostly to herself, because saying it out loud made it feel real. Shabbat ended when the ceremony began, and the ceremony began when the sky was dark enough.

Their father limped over with the spice box, the besamim, and set it on the table. "My knee is not a legitimate excuse to skip the singing," he said, tapping the brace on his leg. "The doctor says the cartilage is worn, which means I sit, it does not mean I am silent."

"The singing is my favorite part," the brother grumbled, but he stayed at the window anyway, because the race still mattered to him even if he pretended it didn't. That was the thing Lauren noticed about him: he changed his mind about Shabbat the way the sky changed at dusk, slowly, and then all at once.

Then he shouted. "One!" He pointed so hard he knocked his knuckle against the glass. Lauren squinted. There, above the neighbor's roof, one small point of light. Her heart started going fast. She scanned the darkening sky, left to right, up and down. "Two!" she called, finding a second star above the maple tree, and they both went silent, hunting.

The third one hid. A wisp of cloud slid over the spot where she was almost sure she had seen something. Lauren held her breath. The cloud thinned, and there it was, faint but definite, three stars exactly where the sky had hidden them.

"Havdalah!" her brother yelled, and their father laughed and poured the wine and lit the braided candle, and the blue flame bobbed in the dark window while they all sang, and Lauren cupped her hands over the spices and breathed in.

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Correlation does not prove causation: two things rising together, like ice cream sales and sunburns, may both be caused by something else, such as hot weather.
story:
Elliot stood in line at the pharmacy behind his neighbour, Mr. Smith, clutching a box of Brain Boost gummies he had found on a shelf between the cough drops and the shampoo. The box said that kids who took Brain Boost every morning got better grades, and there was a photograph of a smiling boy holding a report card with three A's on it. Elliot had a math test on Friday, and a C on his last one, so the box felt like it weighed more than it did.

"Buying those?" Mr. Smith asked, glancing down at him. "My grandson swears by them."

"That's two people," Elliot said slowly, counting on his fingers. "The boy on the box, and your grandson." He looked at the photograph again. The boy was smiling in a tidy kitchen with fruit in a bowl and a stack of books on the counter. That was when a thought landed in Elliot's head like a dropped coin. Kids who take fancy gummies might be kids whose parents buy them books and fruit too. The gummies and the good grades could both come from the same home.

He tried to articulate the idea out loud. "Like ice cream sales and sunburns," he said. "They both go up together, but ice cream doesn't cause sunburn. Hot weather causes both." He had read that in a library book about statistics last summer, and it had stuck with him better than most things he was supposed to remember, like the location of the equator for geography class. "Correlation does not prove causation," he added, saying the words carefully, the way the book had printed them.

Mr. Smith raised an eyebrow but said nothing more, which Elliot appreciated, because he wanted to test it himself. On Friday morning he skipped the gummies and instead ate a proper breakfast, packed his calculator, and did the three practice problems his friend Christopher had texted him the night before. When the tests came back the following week, Elliot had a B plus, one point higher than Christopher, who had taken Brain Boost every morning for a month.

"So the gummies don't work?" Christopher asked in the hallway, turning his test paper over as if the answer might be on the back.

"They might," Elliot said. "I just can't tell yet. All I know is the kids in those ads probably had a lot of other things going on too." He slid his own test into his binder, next to a robust stack of corrected homework, and zipped it shut. "Buy me an ice cream and we'll call it research."

activity: to track how a symbol changes meaning across the chapters of a novel
knowledge_domain: to track how a symbol changes meaning across the chapters of a novel
fact: In Nathaniel Hawthorne's The Scarlet Letter, published in 1850, Hester Prynne's scarlet A begins as a mark of shame, but years later many townspeople say it stands for Able.
story:
Norah slid into the seat behind Makai, dropped her backpack on the floor, and opened her copy of The Scarlet Letter right on her knees. The bus rattled away from the school, and the pages trembled with it.

"I don't get the project," Makai said, twisting around over the seat back. "Mr. Wanjiru wants us to track a symbol, but the letter A is just a letter. It can't change."

"It can," Norah said, but her stomach was not sure. The assignment sheet in her folder said to follow one symbol from the beginning of the book to the end, and write down what it meant each time it appeared. She had read the whole thing, mostly, and she remembered that the townspeople at the start treated Hester Prynne's scarlet A like a brand. It marked her shame. Everyone in the settlement stared at it. That part was easy. The ending was fog.

She flipped to her first sticky note, the one on the scaffold scene, where the crowd hissed at Hester and the A glowed on her chest. She wrote on it: "To the town, the A means shame. Page one, basically." Then she turned to the last chapters, and there it was, plain as the window beside her. Years had passed in the story. Hester had spent them quietly helping people, and near the end many of the townspeople said the A stood for something else entirely.

"Able," Norah said out loud.

"What?"

"That's the word. Near the end, many townspeople say the A stands for Able. It stopped meaning shame and started meaning that. Same letter, different meaning, because of what Hester did with her life." She wrote it on a fresh sticky note and lined it up beside the first one on the bus window, where the morning light made both notes glow like little signal flags. "The letter never changes. The people change."

Makai frowned at the two notes. "So a symbol is like a vase that inherits whatever you put in it?"

"Sort of. Like the American flag, or a word. It means whatever the people around it decide it means." Norah tapped the second note. "First amendment to my theory: I thought symbols were one thing forever. Wrong."

At the next stop, Youcef climbed on with his own copy of the book under his arm, looking pale and miserable. He had the flu last week and was two chapters behind, and tomorrow the notes were due. Norah saw him hesitate in the aisle, and she knew that feeling, being the vulnerable one who missed everything.

She pulled her two sticky notes off the window and held them up before he even sat down. "Start here. It's the whole project in two notes. First the A means shame, then Able. Copy them and give them back."

Youcef sat down beside Makai, took out a pencil, and started writing, while the bus rolled on toward home.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Oil paint does not dry by water evaporating; its oil slowly reacts with oxygen in the air, so an oil painting can take days or longer to dry to the touch.
story:
Isaac pressed his fingertip against the corner of his painting for the third time that morning, and for the third time the blue paint squished under it like frosting. The art cabin at Camp Silver Birch smelled of linseed oil and pine, and outside the window Kasen was already packing his duffel, because today was the last day.

"I have to carry mine home this afternoon," Blanche said, holding up her canvas, a sunset over the lake. "My mom's picking me up at four." She fanned it with a clipboard, then set it in front of the little window fan. Isaac watched the paint stay exactly as shiny as before. He frowned. The fan had been blowing on his painting since breakfast too, and it hadn't helped one bit.

He thought about how the cabins worked. The thermostat on the wall made the heater run until the room got warm, but heat hadn't helped either, because Mr. Tang kept the cabin cool and the paint was still wet. Water drying was fast, like the watercolor bowls from Tuesday, which had dried before lunch. So why was the oil paint so obstinate? Maybe it wasn't water at all. He tried an experiment. He covered half his canvas with the lid of a plastic tub, sealing it tight, and left the other half open in the air.

By lunch the uncovered half was tackier, just barely, and the covered half had not changed at all. That meant the paint needed the open air somehow, not moving air, not heat. He asked Mr. Tang only one question: "Does oil paint use water?" Mr. Tang shook his head. "No evaporation. The oil reacts with oxygen, and it can take days, sometimes longer, before it's dry to the touch."

"Days?" Blanche said, her shoulders dropping.

"Then we can't drive them home loose," Isaac said. He dug under the supply shelf and found two flat pieces of cardboard and some wooden stir sticks. He built a shallow box around Blanche's sunset so nothing could touch the surface, then made one for his own. Kasen carried them to the pickup area flat and level, like a waiter with two trays.

At four o'clock Blanche's mom leaned the boxes carefully against the back seat, and Blanche grinned through the window. "Text me when yours is finally dry!"

activity: to explain how sound travels as vibrations and why it moves faster through water than air
knowledge_domain: to explain how sound travels as vibrations and why it moves faster through water than air
fact: Sound travels faster in warm air than in cold air, gaining about 0.6 meters per second for each degree Celsius.
story:
Sawyer pressed his ear against the tube in the sound room of the science museum and counted under his breath. The exhibit, a long pipe with a microphone at each end, was supposed to let visitors time how long a click took to travel from one side to the other. Ria stood at the far end, ready to tap.

"Go," he called, and she knocked twice on the pipe's cap.

He had measured once already in the cool morning, when the museum had just opened, and the click had taken a certain fraction of a second, showing on the little screen as a number he'd written in his notebook. Now it was afternoon, the room had warmed up, and the sun through the skylight made the metal pipe almost hot to touch. He tapped the screen to reset and waited for Ria's second knock. The new number was smaller. Faster. He ran it twice more, and both times the click arrived sooner than it had that morning. Why would heat change a sound?

"Maybe the pipe's lying," Ria said, walking back to him. "Machines glitch."

"That's the pessimistic way to look at it," Sawyer said. "I think it's a real pattern. Warm room, faster click. Cold room, slower click." He checked the thermometer hanging on the wall beside the exhibit. It had climbed six degrees since his first measurement. He did some arithmetic in the margin of his page, tongue between his teeth, then crossed it out and revised his figure, because he had divided where he should have multiplied. The differences matched something close to a rule: about 0.6 meters per second faster for every degree Celsius warmer the air got.

Ms. Warsame, the guide, drifted past with a cart of spare microphones. Sawyer stopped her. "So sound travels faster in warm air than in cold air," he said. "About point six meters per second for each degree?"

She smiled and pointed at a second tube, a fat one filled with water, with two earpieces on long cords. "Try that one," she said.

Sawyer pressed the earpiece to his ear while Ria rapped the underwater hammer, and the knock arrived almost before he could start counting.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: Spanish generally uses "ser" for lasting traits and "estar" for temporary states: "Mi hermano es alto" means he is tall, while "Mi hermano está cansado" means he is tired.
story:
Hunter stared at the blank line on his worksheet and wished, for the third time that morning, that he had paid more attention on Tuesday. Mr. Goldberg's classroom smelled like pencil shavings, and outside the window the big oak's canopy threw moving shadows across the desks. "Describe your family in five full sentences," the assignment said, "in Spanish."

He had started okay. Mi mamá es maestra. That one felt solid. Then Mi perro es pequeno, because Biscuit really was small and would stay small forever. But when he got to his older brother Marcus, Hunter wrote what he thought was harmless: Mi hermano está cansado. He copied it onto his sentence strip and moved on, planning to convert his rough notes into a final draft at home.

At lunch, Mckenna grabbed the strip out of his binder before he could stop her. "Since when is Marcus tired all the time?" she asked, grinning.

"He's not. He's just tired from practice."

"Then why does your sentence say he is?" Lorelai leaned over Mckenna's shoulder, chewing the end of her pretzel. "That's what my cousin told me last summer. Spanish has two words for 'is.' You used the wrong one."

Hunter took the strip back and studied it. Two words for one little verb seemed ridiculous, like having two words for "dog." But he remembered the practice sentences from Monday, the ones Mr. Goldberg had written on the board: Mi hermano es alto and, right under it, Mi hermano está cansado. Same brother, two different verbs. Why would a teacher do that unless the verbs weren't the same at all?

He laid his own sentences out on the lunch table like evidence. Mi mamá es maestra: always true, no taking that back. Mi perro es pequeno: permanent too. Marcus being tired: that would change the minute he slept till noon on Saturday. Hunter crossed out está, and something about it bothered him. Last fall he had quit piano after three weeks because a piece looked hard on the first day, and his mom had said maybe try one more lesson before you decide. Maybe he'd quit this verb too fast.

After school he found Mr. Goldberg stacking chairs. "Can I check something?" Hunter held up the strip. "I want to say my brother is tired right now, but not forever."

Mr. Goldberg read it and nodded. "Estar is the one for temporary. Ser is the one for lasting traits. You had it right the first time."

Hunter walked home through the park, where the softball field's dirt had been raked into neat dark rows, fertile ground for next month's games. He thought about Marcus, probably sprawled on the couch, tired today and fine tomorrow. At the kitchen table he rewrote the sentence and added a sixth: Mi hermano es alto, porque that part would never change.

When Marcus wandered in, Hunter slid the paper across to him. "This says you're tall," Marcus said.

"And this one says you're tired," Hunter said. "But only till you stop staying up till midnight."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Many places of worship, including mosques, Hindu temples and Sikh gurdwaras, ask visitors to remove their shoes, and gurdwaras also ask everyone to cover their head.
story:
Ava and Lilianna hurried up the steps of the community hall, where Ava's family had helped enroll volunteers for the harvest celebration at the gurdwara that now filled the main room. The program started at noon, and the clock in the lobby already showed 11:52. Ava stopped so suddenly at the doorway that Lilianna nearly bumped into her.

"Shoes off here," Ava said, pointing to the long rows of shoes on the racks, sneakers and sandals lined up like sleeping animals. Lilianna knelt to unlace her boots, and Ava felt a small knot of guilt tighten in her chest. Last spring she had brought her cousin here without warning her, and her cousin had spent the whole visit barefoot and pink-eared, embarrassed in front of everyone. Ava had told herself it wasn't a big deal, but afterward she wondered whether she simply hadn't thought it mattered, the way people overlook things for guests who aren't quite like them. She had promised herself she wouldn't let that bias creep in again.

"Lilianna, wait." Ava pulled a folded scarf out of her backpack and held it out. "Everyone covers their head here, everybody, not just the people who come all the time. I brought two, just in case." Lilianna wrapped the orange scarf over her hair, tucking it the way Ava showed her, and they stepped through the doors with their shoes left behind on the shelf.

Inside, the hall smelled of cardamom and warm bread. Ava's grandmother, who was one of the most influential volunteers in the kitchen, waved them toward a table near the front. "You made it," she said, glancing at the clock. "Two minutes to spare." Ava slid into a chair beside Lilianna, whose scarf had slipped a little. Lilianna reached up and straightened it herself, then whispered, "Thanks for the extra one."

Ava watched the singers take their places at the front and felt the knot in her chest loosen. The drums began, low and steady, and Lilianna leaned over and asked, "Can we go see the kitchen after?"

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: During Ramadan, Muslims eat a meal called suhur before the dawn prayer, then go without food and drink until sunset.
story:
The alarm went off at 4:37, and Audrey was already awake, which felt almost reckless, because who wakes up before their own alarm on purpose? She padded downstairs in the dark and found her mother setting out eggs, dates, and a big glass of water on the kitchen table.

"Suhur," her mother said, tapping the table. "That's what we call this meal, before the dawn prayer. After that, no food or drink until sunset."

Audrey had a theory. Her first real fast was today, only until mid-afternoon because she was twelve and that was the deal her parents had made, and she figured the smart move was to eat as much as possible now. If the tank was full, she reasoned, it would take longer to run empty, like how Dad turned the thermostat down in winter to conserve heat for the whole day. So she ate three eggs, four dates, two slices of toast, and drank both glasses of water on the table.

By nine o'clock she felt like a balloon. Her stomach ached and her mouth was dry anyway, which made no sense. She had drunk so much water. Where had it gone? She lay on the couch and thought about it, turning the puzzle over. Maybe it was like her science teacher said about rain: you could see the effect without seeing the cause. Maybe the big meal had made her thirstier, not safer. Her theory needed testing, and tomorrow was another day.

That afternoon, the doorbell rang. It was Imogen, holding a foil pan. "My mom sent baklava," she said, grinning. "She heard it's your first fast. Also, I'm doing the afternoon part with you tomorrow, so, you know, solidarity."

Audrey sat up so fast the couch cushion slid. "Wait, really? Then tomorrow we test something. Half the food, more water, and we'll see who makes it longer."

Imogen dropped onto the couch beside her and stole the corner piece of baklava. "Deal. But if my way wins, you carry my backpack for a week."

Audrey shook her hand, then pointed at the last pastry. "That one's mine at sunset."

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: All 50 U.S. states, and Washington, D.C., have passed laws on handling concussions in youth sports.
story:
Christopher stood at the edge of the pool, toes curled over the rough tile, and watched the boy in lane three climb out slowly. That was the strange part. The boy, a descendant of the school's fastest swimmer from twenty years ago, had smacked his head on the starting block during a dive, and now the coach was waving him out of the water instead of shouting at him to go again. At every other tryout Christopher had ever seen, the coach pushed people to fight through things. Something invisible had to be behind this.

He remembered last spring, when his cousin got pulled from a soccer game after a hard fall and nobody could explain the rule to him. It happened in every sport, Christopher realized, and in every state they had lived in, even when they moved from Ohio to Oregon. It was like a pattern hiding in plain sight. Maybe it wasn't a coach's mood or a team rule. Maybe it was something bigger, something that followed them wherever they went.

"Oceane," he whispered to the girl waiting beside him, "did you see that? Why did he have to stop?" Oceane shrugged. "My mom says it's not just our school. All fifty states have laws about concussions in youth sports. Even Washington, D.C." Christopher blinked. Laws, not rules. That was why no coach could argue, even the controversial ones who benched kids for looking at them wrong.

When Christopher's turn came, he dove clean and fast, arms slicing the water, and touched the wall with his fingertips stinging. He climbed out, heart pounding, and the coach looked at the stopwatch for a long moment. "You want to nominate yourself for the relay team?" the coach asked. "Because that was the second-fastest time all day."

Christopher glanced down the row of soaked, shivering kids, then back at the coach. "Yes," he said. "I'd like that."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: In Hungarian, a person's family name is written before the given name, the same order used in Chinese, Japanese and Korean names.
story:
The card sat on the dessert table between the plum cake and a bowl of walnuts, signed in careful blue ink: "Fekete László." Mia read it three times. She was at Lyra's grandmother's birthday party because Lyra had invited her whole class and only three people had come, so Mia felt she owed the afternoon to friendship and free cake. But the signature bothered her. Lyra's grandfather's name was László. Everybody called him that, all afternoon, so who was Fekete?

"You think he signed somebody else's card," Lyra said, cracking a walnut with her palm. "That's wild."

"Or he made a mistake. Grandfathers make mistakes." Mia had watched her own grandfather insist for an hour that the TV remote was a phone.

Edison leaned over the card with his mouth full of cake. "Or it's a secret code. Like a spy."

Lyra opposed the spy theory immediately, on the grounds that spies did not sign birthday cards in ballpoint at parties. She proposed asking him, and Mia proposed watching first, because if he had made a mistake she did not want to embarrass him in front of twenty relatives eating strudel.

So Mia tested it. The gift table held four other envelopes. She carried them to the hallway where nobody tripped on her and read every signature. One said "Nagy Erzsébet," which was Lyra's grandmother, whose name was definitely Erzsébet. Another said "Szabó Péter," and Mia knew Uncle Péter had told the honey joke at dinner. Every single card put the family name first.

"Lyra," she whispered. "They're all backwards. On purpose, I think."

They found the grandfather in the kitchen, carving a tiny wooden bird with a pocketknife, which Lyra said he did at every party because he was a real artisan and could not sit still. Mia held out the card.

"Sir, did you mean to sign it like this, family name first?"

He looked up, and his whole face folded into a smile. "In Hungarian, the family name comes before the given name," he said. "The same order as Chinese, Japanese and Korean names."

Mia blinked. She had a classmate named Chen Wei, and everyone called him Wei, because Chen came first and was the family name. The pattern had been sitting in her own classroom the whole time.

"So you're Fekete like Chen is Chen," she said.

"Exactly so." He went back to the bird.

Edison arrived, breathless, holding the last envelope. "I figured out the code," he announced. "It's Hungarian."

"We know," said Lyra.

"You're all gullible," Edison said, "I made that up an hour ago and you believed me."

Mia took the wooden bird when the grandfather offered it, turning it over in her hand, and slid it into her pocket next to the napkin she had wrapped around a second piece of cake.

activity: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
knowledge_domain: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
fact: Circuit diagrams show current flowing from positive to negative, but the electrons in the wires actually move from negative to positive.
story:
Brayden's circuit had one job, and the bulb refused to do it. He had taped the battery, the switch, and the bulb to a board covered in red paper, and the arrows on his diagram marched confidently from the positive end of the battery around to the negative end. That was what the book showed. But the book's arrows were, he would soon learn, the least of his problems.

"The bulb's not dead, I tested it in my residence last night with a battery from the TV remote," said River, holding the little glass dome up to the gym lights. Emilio tapped the switch with one finger, then two fingers, as if gentle mediation between Brayden and the machine might help. "It clicks," Emilio reported. "Very satisfying click. No light, though." Brayden followed each wire with his eyes, then with an elastic band snapped around his wrist for luck. Somewhere in this loop, he thought, something invisible was failing. Electricity was the one thing in his project nobody could actually watch.

He found it. The wire from the switch to the bulb had slipped loose under the tape, so the loop was broken, and when he pressed it back on with his thumb, the bulb blazed so brightly that Emilio yelped and knocked over a cup of pencils. "Electricity goes around the whole loop," Brayden said, grinning. "Break it anywhere, nothing flows." Ms. Szabó, judging the row, leaned in and asked which way the current moved, and Brayden pointed at his arrows. "Positive to negative. Like the diagram." River shook her head slowly, the way she did when she was about to enjoy herself. "The diagram's arrows are the convention, but the electrons actually move the other way, from negative to positive. The book even says so. Page forty."

Brayden stared at his board, then at the glowing bulb, then at the arrows he had spent an hour drawing. "So my diagram points the wrong way, and it's still right?" River shrugged. "Congratulations. You built something that works and confuses people." Emilio raised the cup of pencils like a trophy. Brayden flipped his marker open and added, in careful letters beneath the arrows, "The electrons went the other way the whole time."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: The NFL's passer rating combines several passing statistics into one number on a scale from 0 to a maximum of 158.3.
story:
Felix had one quarter left to figure it out, and the basketball game was not helping. He sat in the bleachers between Eliana and Julianna, watching the home team's point guard dribble through traffic, and all he could think about was a number his older cousin had said on the couch last night: 158.3. "That's a perfect passer rating," his cousin had told him, "in football. Not 100. One hundred fifty-eight point three." Felix had spent half the night wondering why anybody would calibrate a scale so that perfect landed on a number like that. It felt like a ruler where the last mark was at eleven and three quarters.

"Focus," Eliana said, elbowing him. "Devon's about to shoot."

Devon, their classmate and the shortest kid on the court, lofted a three that bounced off the back rim. The crowd groaned. Felix groaned too, but part of his brain was still at work. Sports were full of squished-together numbers. The scoreboard said the home team was shooting 44 percent, which meant misses and makes from the whole game, pressed into one tidy figure. The announcer said Devon was averaging nine points a game, even though last game he had scored two and the game before he had scored nineteen. Nobody kept the whole story. They kept the summary.

"Okay, I have a theory," Felix announced during a timeout. "Numbers in sports are like juice concentrate. All the events get squeezed down, and you only see one number at the end."

"That's not a theory," said Julianna, who wanted to be a scientist and policed the word. "That's a metaphor."

"It's a hypothesis," Felix said. "And here's the test. Ask my cousin's football thing. Perfect passer rating. What number do you guess?"

Eliana squinted. "A hundred."

Julianna said, "A hundred, obviously. Percent means out of a hundred."

"158.3," Felix said, and let it sit there. He had checked it three times this morning, scrolling on his mom's phone at breakfast until she made him put the jam away and eat like a person. The scale ran from zero all the way up to a maximum of 158.3, and a perfect passer landed exactly on that strange top mark. It combined a bunch of passing numbers into one, like the scoreboard squeezed all the shots into a percentage. He could not see why. He only knew that it was true, and that knowing it felt like holding a secret with a rough edge.

"A hundred fifty-eight point three," Julianna repeated slowly, as if tasting something sour. "That's significant. That's a weird, specific, significant number."

"Maybe whoever built it didn't want perfect to feel easy," Eliana said. "Like, you have to earn a number with three decimal places."

Down on the court, Devon stole the ball, sprinted alone toward the hoop, and missed the layup so badly it hit the bottom of the backboard. But he was grinning as he ran back on defense, and the crowd, out of pure loyalty, cheered the miss like a dunk. Felix laughed until his sides hurt, and somewhere in his head the erosion of his old assumption finished its work: he no longer believed every number was built to be friendly.

"Next timeout," he said, "we're ranking the players by who has the weirdest stat. Devon's already winning."

"Devon's always winning that one," Eliana said, and the buzzer sounded for the fourth quarter.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Psychologists often separate fear, a reaction to a threat happening now, from anxiety, worry about a threat that might happen in the future.
story:
Charlotte pushed her noodles around the plate while her mother talked about the geese that migrate over their town every October, how they somehow know to leave before the cold arrives. Charlotte barely heard her. The soccer tryout was on Thursday, and it was only Monday.

"You've hardly touched dinner," her mother said.

"I keep thinking about Thursday," Charlotte admitted. "My stomach hurts, but only when I think about it. That's weird, right?"

Her little brother started making ghost noises at her from across the table, and she put up her hand. "Stop. That's a boundary. I mean it." He stopped, mostly because he wanted more noodles.

Charlotte remembered something Mr. Vu had said last spring, when a thunderstorm rolled in during their field trip and half the class dove under the picnic tables. Afterward, while they were brushing leaves off their jackets, he had told them, "Fear is what you feel when something scary is happening right now. Anxiety is worry about something that might happen later." Nobody had been diving under tables on a sunny day. The diving came with the actual thunder.

So she ran a little test on herself. Was a thunderstorm happening at the dinner table? No. Was the tryout happening? Also no. Thursday was three whole days away, and she was sitting in a chair, safe, with noodles. Yet her heart was pounding like the threat was right in front of her. Her body, she realized, could not tell the difference between now and later. Her mind had dragged Thursday into Monday evening, like a bird that left too early and got caught in the storm anyway.

That gave her an idea about what to do. If the threat wasn't actually here, maybe she could send it back where it belonged. She set down her fork, breathed in for four counts and out for four, and told her mother, "This is how I'm coping. My counselor taught it to me." Her stress didn't vanish, but the pounding slowed, like something landing.

"The tryout sounds like a big deal," her mother said. "Is that why Elliott texted you six times?"

Charlotte checked her phone. Elliott had sent a message with an intricate diagram of the tryout drills, drawn in blue ink, arrows everywhere, plus a note that read, "My mom's corporation just transferred her, so if I make the team I can still stay at this school." He was worried about the future too, only his future was even more tangled than hers.

She typed back: Nothing scary is happening right this second. We're both just eating dinner. Then, out loud to her mother, she said, "Can I have more noodles? Thursday me will need the energy, but Monday me gets to eat it."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: In 1913 Max Ringelmann reported that as more people pulled on a rope together, each person's average pull became smaller.
story:
At the community center gym, Coach blew the whistle and split the tug-of-war teams into four, then five, then six players on each side. Rosalie wrapped the rope around her gloves and pulled until her shoulders burned.
