Afterward, while everyone crowded around the water fountain, she noticed Parker rubbing his palms and staring at the rope like it had lied to him.

"We pulled harder when there were four of us," he said. "I'm sure of it. Six people should beat four easily, but it didn't feel that way."

Rosalie chewed the strap of her goggles and thought about it. It was like the time the whole class got quiet because everyone assumed someone else would answer the teacher's question. Maybe pulling worked the same way. She couldn't see effort directly, so she borrowed a lens to examine it: the gym's old spring scale, the kind Mr. Suryanto kept in the storage closet for the fitness unit. If each person pulled alone, then in pairs, then in fours, the scale would show the truth hiding inside the group's total.

She asked Cecelia and Parker to help after practice. Alone, Rosalie pulled the scale to eighteen. In a pair with Cecelia, the needle climbed, but less than the sum of their solo pulls. In a group of four, it was worse. Each extra person added less and less, as if the pull itself were thinning out.

Rosalie found the answer in the community center's small library, in a dusty book about the science of work. She read the page twice, then held it up to her friends. "In 1913, Max Ringelmann reported that as more people pulled on a rope together, each person's average pull became smaller." She tried to paraphrase it in her head: bigger group, lazier average pull, every single time.

"So it wasn't just us feeling tired," Parker said.

"It's a real thing. It happens to everyone." Rosalie wasn't vain about figuring it out; she was just glad it wasn't a flaw in their team.

At the next practice, she counted off in fours, kept the groups small, and shouted, "Pull like you're alone out there!" The rope snapped sideways, and Coach's team went down in the dust.

activity: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
knowledge_domain: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
fact: Puberty is driven by hormones: the pituitary gland in the brain signals the ovaries or testes to make more estrogen or testosterone.
story:
Alexis raised her hand halfway and then put it down, because asking the whole class why she suddenly smelled like a wet dog after gym was not something she was brave enough to do. She had never needed deodorant before this year. In third grade she could run four laps and smell like nothing. Now she ran one lap and Emmet sat a seat away from her in science, which was a message she could read perfectly well.

At lunch she brought it up to Caius, quietly, under the noise of the cafeteria. "Did you change? Like, your smell?" Caius nodded like it was the least embarrassing question in the world. "My mom bought me the green deodorant. It works, mostly." Alexis had a theory forming, the same intuition she got in math when a problem had a hidden step. Something must have flipped a switch inside her, because third-grade Alexis and fifth-grade Alexis had the same soap and the same towel. The change had to come from a signal she couldn't see.

She remembered her checkup in September. She had asked the doctor what actually tells the body it's time for puberty, and the doctor had drawn a little arrow on a diagram. Alexis repeated it now, tapping her own forehead. "The pituitary gland, right here in the brain, sends the signal. It tells the ovaries or the testes to make more estrogen or testosterone." Caius chewed his sandwich. "So my brain is sending me smelly emails." "Basically," Alexis said. "And that's also why the sweat sits longer and the bacteria decompose it, and decomposing stuff is the smell." Caius waved his pizza. "Like a dinosaur going extinct, but for your armpits staying clean. Gone forever."

After school Alexis walked to the corner store and counted her allowance on the counter. The cashier raised an eyebrow at her exact sixty-two cents. "It's science," Alexis said. The next day she ran her lap, showered in the gym changing room without hiding it, and slid into her science seat with room to spare. Emmet leaned over. "You smell like a pine forest." "I know," Alexis said. "I planted it."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Pencil 'lead' has never contained the metal lead; the name comes from early writers mistaking graphite for a kind of lead ore.
story:
Ariana pressed her pencil against the sketchbook, shading the wing of a paper dragon she was building at the craft table under the big striped tent. The dragon's body would be folded cardboard, painted with an intricate pattern of scales, but the wings needed to look delicate, and pencil shading before paint seemed like the best trick. Lucille sat across from her, folding scales out of old magazine pages, and Hudson was testing which glue held the tail spikes on longest.

Then came the problem. A little boy from the youngest cabin, maybe seven, stood at the edge of the table with tears streaking his cheeks, clutching a pencil like it was a snake. "I sucked on my pencil," he whispered. "I'm going to be poisoned. My brother said so. He said lead kills you."

Ariana looked at the pencil, then at her half-shaded wing, and something tickled the back of her mind. She remembered a line from a book she'd read three times, waiting for her turn on the pottery wheel. "Wait," she said. "You're not poisoned. Pencil lead has never contained the metal lead." The boy blinked at her. "It's not lead at all," she went on. "The name comes from early writers mistaking graphite for a kind of lead ore. Graphite. That's all that's in there. You basically ate rock dust and clay."

"Rock dust," the boy repeated. He still looked wobbly, so Ariana decided to test it. She went to Mr. Flores, who ran the craft tent and kept a box of spare supplies, and asked to see a pencil and the jar of broken leads. She snapped a lead in half for the boy to examine. It was silvery and slippery, and it left a shine on his finger, nothing like a heavy dull metal. Mr. Flores handed her a note another camper had left at the supply box that morning. She read it out loud: "Ariana, if you find my grey polymer eraser, please save it for dragon wings. I read they are the opposite of poison. Your dragon looks so cool already." The whole table laughed, even the little boy.

Ariana gave the boy a fresh pencil and told him to anticipate a great dragon, because by dinner the whole tent was going to want one. He sat down next to her, and Lucille showed him how to fold his first scale. He drew a tiny dragon of his own, wobbly-winged and grinning, and Ariana shaded its tail with careful grey strokes.

activity: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
knowledge_domain: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
fact: In the United States, a bill must pass both the House of Representatives and the Senate in identical form before it goes to the president.
story:
Hannah had a civics quiz on Monday, and she was spending the weekend at her grandpa's house, where the only study materials were a giant dictionary, an ancient globe, and Grandpa's newspaper. She spread the paper across the kitchen table and stared at an article about a bill in Congress. "It says the bill passed the House," she muttered, "but then it says the Senate has its own version. So which one becomes the law? The one that got more votes? The one that's longer?"

Grandpa, who was washing a teapot that was already clean, snorted. "You think laws work like a limbo contest? Lowest bill wins?"

"Grandpa, this is serious. If I flunk this quiz, I have to retake it in front of the whole class." She flipped the page and found another article, an older one, about the same bill. The House version and the Senate version were different. In one, a sentence had been added; in the other, a word had been changed. That was her clue. It wasn't about winning or size. The versions had to match.

She grabbed the dictionary, not to look up a word but to prop up her phone, and searched until she found it: a bill must pass both the House of Representatives and the Senate in identical form before it goes to the president. Both. Identical. She tested the idea against the articles, holding one up beside the other like a detective comparing handwriting. The older article showed mismatched versions and no law. The newer one showed the Senate agreeing to the House's exact wording, and suddenly everyone was talking about what the president would do.

To demonstrate it, she lined up Grandpa's teacups on the counter. "This row is the House, this row is the Senate. If the cups match, the bill goes to the president. If they don't, nothing happens. No matching cups, no law." Grandpa added a sugar bowl to the end of the line and said, "And that's the president." He studied the rows gravely. "It's very logical. Although I still think my limbo theory had style."

Hannah laughed so hard she nearly knocked over the sugar bowl. It wasn't a hierarchy of smart people passing down wisdom; she had figured it out herself, with a newspaper and two mismatched teacups. She picked up the sugar bowl and marched it to the end of the counter, announcing, "The president signs it. It's a law."

"Then I move," Grandpa said, raising his actual teacup, "that we celebrate with cookies."

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
fact: Fingers, toes, ears and the nose are the parts of the body most likely to get frostbite.
story:
The snow had come down all night, and when Easton looked out his window at seven in the morning, the street had vanished under a white blanket and school was cancelled. He whooped so loudly that his dad stumbled in with a toaster, thinking something was wrong. Within an hour Easton was dragging his sled to the hill behind Jada's house, where Jada and Emmett were already arguing about who had the faster run.

Easton wore gloves and boots but had left his hat on the kitchen table, which nobody remembered until his ears went strange, like they belonged to a snowman loaned to him temporarily. "I can't feel them," he announced, patting the sides of his head. Emmett laughed and said he must have exceptional ears, so special they numbed themselves. Jada did not laugh. She pulled off her own hat and jammed it onto his head. "My mom's a nurse," she said. "Fingers, toes, ears, and the nose are the parts of the body most likely to get frostbite. That's just how it is."

Easton tested this idea the way he tested everything, which had once sustained an entire afternoon of dropping marshmallows from the garage roof to see which surfaces they bounced on. He wiggled his fingers, still warm inside his gloves. He wiggled his toes, cozy in his boots. Then he touched his nose, which felt cold as a fence post. It was true. Everything uncovered, at the edges of him, was freezing first, while the middle of him was fine. Last winter Emmett had spent a whole sled day with no hat and had come home with ears so red his mom thought he'd painted them, and now Easton understood that Emmett hadn't just been dramatic, though he was also definitely that.

"Ten more runs," Emmett begged.

"One run," said Jada, "and you wear this scarf over your nose, or I drag you home by it."

Emmett wrapped the scarf around his face until only his eyes showed, which made him look like a very polite bank robber, and said, "Behold, a diplomat of winter."

They took the last run together, all three on one sled, and crashed into the drift at the bottom in a spray of snow.

activity: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
knowledge_domain: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
fact: In front crawl, swimmers breathe out underwater through the mouth and nose, so they only need a quick breath in when the face turns to the side.
story:
Hannah's whole plan for Saturday was to submerge her face in the school pool, swim twenty-five metres of front crawl, and breathe like a normal fish. The fish part was the problem. Every time she turned her head to the side, she tried to breathe out and then in during that one quick turn, and she swallowed half the pool. She coughed, Demi patted her back, and Gemma offered her a chlorine-flavoured granola bar, which Hannah suspected was a joke.

They lived in an affluent town with a fancy new pool, and Mr. Sadeghi ran the Saturday club, but he mostly stood at the far end with a clipboard and let them figure things out. "Twenty-five metres by March," he had said once, and that was all.

Hannah lay on the bench and thought while Gemma counted ceiling tiles. The problem couldn't be the turning. Demi turned the same amount and breathed fine. So there had to be something happening underwater, where Hannah couldn't watch it. Maybe Demi wasn't doing two things during her turn. Maybe she was only doing one. That would explain why her turn could be so short and still work. Hannah needed evidence.

She dunked her face in and watched Demi swim a whole lap underwater-near-the-surface, goggles on. Bubbles. Streams of bubbles came out of Demi's mouth and nose the entire time her face was down. Then Demi turned, took one quick sip of air, and put her face right back in. Out underwater, in at the side. That was it. She wasn't faster; she just wasn't wasting her turn.

Hannah pushed off the wall for another try. Face down, hum bubbles out through mouth and nose, turn, quick breath in, face down again. Somewhere around fifteen metres she realized she wasn't coughing. By twenty she was grinning underwater, which let more water in than expected, but she kept going. She slapped the far wall and stood up.

"You didn't drown," said Gemma.

"Truce with the pool," Hannah said, spitting out a little water. "For now."

Mr. Sadeghi wrote something on his clipboard. Hannah decided not to find out what until she could swim fifty.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: In email, BCC stands for 'blind carbon copy': people added in the BCC field receive the message, but other recipients cannot see their addresses.
story:
Jaxson climbed onto the school bus holding his tablet like a pizza with extra cheese, flat and careful, because the group project email was due before first period. Daniyal slid over to make room, peering at the screen.

"You're inviting the whole class to your birthday thing?" Daniyal said. "That's like thirty addresses in one email."

"Ms. Pham said we could use the tablets for club stuff," Jaxson said. "It counts. Anyway, I'm not typing them all."

He typed the invitation, then hit one wrong key and the address list vanished. The email still said "To: whole class," somehow, but every single name had disappeared into a mysterious field labeled BCC. Jaxson stared at it. He tried sending a test message to himself and Daniyal, putting Daniyal's address in the BCC line, and when Daniyal's phone buzzed, the message showed only Jaxson's name at the top.

"It's like a secret handshake," Jaxson said. "BCC means blind carbon copy. They get it, but nobody else can see their addresses."

"That's a paradox," Daniyal said, licking a pretend wound. "You invite everyone and yet you tell nobody who everyone is. My brain needs a minute to digest this."

"Your brain needs a minute to digest everything. You once thought recess was a food."

Hayden leaned over the seat behind them, waving her phone. "Wait, is this the lake party? Because the whole class voted and it was unanimous, everyone wants the chocolate cake, not the ice cream cake."

Hayden's want was simple and famous: she intended to be the first to know everything, and she'd been sulking ever since the bus driver had refused to install Wi-Fi. "If you send that email with everyone's addresses showing," she warned, "Marcus will reply-all forty times. Forty. He did it to the soccer list."

Jaxson hit send with the BCC field full and the To line empty of classmates, and the bus rumbled over the pothole by the gym while twenty-nine phones began buzzing at once, like a nest of very polite bees.

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: The 2019 Scripps National Spelling Bee ended with eight co-champions, because the spellers kept getting every word right.
story:
Justin stood behind the little table in the meeting room of the public library, his word list face down in front of him like a dare. The regional spelling bee was still three weeks away, and Mr. Sow, the librarian, had set up a practice bee every Saturday so the spellers could get used to saying letters out loud in front of people. Vanessa sat two chairs down, whispering vowels to herself. Tatum had his headphones on, eyes shut, mouthing something that looked like "migrate," which was the word that had knocked him out last year.

The problem was the trophy. There was only one, a small gold bee on a wooden base, and it went to the first-place speller. Justin had come second at everything that year, second in the science fair, second in the fun run, and the feeling had started to follow him around like a shadow. He wanted the trophy so badly that he had worked out a whole algorithm for studying: fifteen minutes of spelling, five minutes of definition, repeat until dinner. But Vanessa was studying too, and she never missed.

That morning he found a folded note tucked inside his returned library book, in Vanessa's careful handwriting. "I heard you get nervous when it comes down to two spellers. Me too. Want to practice sudden-death rounds together instead of alone? Also, look up what happened at the 2019 national bee. It made me feel better. Vanessa."

Justin pulled the newspaper archive off the shelf near the opaque glass windows of the study room and typed in the year. The headline came up fast, and he read it twice. The 2019 Scripps National Spelling Bee had ended with eight co-champions, because the spellers kept getting every word right. Eight kids, one title, all of them winners at the same time. He sat very still, letting it sink in. It was not a rule or a trick. It was just what had happened when nobody missed.

At practice that afternoon, it came down to Justin and Vanessa, round after round. "Peregrine," said Mr. Sow. "P-E-R-E-G-R-I-N-E," said Justin. Vanessa spelled "ricochet" without a blink. Round nineteen arrived, and Mr. Sow looked at his card, then at the clock, and then at the two of them standing there, both still perfect.

"You know," Justin said to Vanessa, half whispering, "in 2019 the national bee ended with eight co-champions, because the spellers kept getting every word right." Vanessa's eyes widened. "Eight?"

Mr. Sow raised his hand like a referee. "Then here is my ruling. We have reached the end of our word list. Justin and Vanessa, you are both declared practice champions today." He set the little gold bee on the shelf between their two chairs, and Justin slid it an inch toward Vanessa, and she slid it right back.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: The hongi is a traditional Maori greeting in New Zealand in which two people press their noses and foreheads together, symbolizing the sharing of the breath of life.
story:
Hazel stood at the edge of the reception hall in her stiff new shoes, watching the line of guests move toward the groom's aunties. The wedding had already conquered her whole morning, first a turbulent ferry ride across the harbour during which she had gripped the seat, then the ceremony on the beach beside a carved wooden hull mounted on blocks like a boat frozen mid-voyage. Now came the part she had been dreading. She was supposed to greet the groom's family, who had flown in from New Zealand, and she had no idea how.

Lainey nudged her. "You're up after Sage."

Sage walked forward confidently, stuck out her hand, and said, "Congratulations." The eldest auntie smiled, took the hand gently, and then leaned in and pressed her nose and forehead against Sage's. Sage went rigid. Hazel's stomach flipped. Whatever she had planned to do was clearly wrong, and she could not see the rule behind it. Was it only for elders? Only for women? She watched the next guest, a tall uncle, receive the same pressing of noses and forehead, and then a small cousin, no older than seven, get it too. Family and strangers, young and old. So it was for everyone.

"Go on," Lainey whispered.

Hazel stepped up to the auntie. Instead of offering her hand, she leaned forward and touched her nose and forehead to the auntie's. For a second she held her breath, certain she had guessed wrong. Then the auntie pulled back, beaming, and said something to the others that made them laugh warmly.

"She did the hongi," Sage hissed behind her. "How did you know?"

"I watched," Hazel whispered. "Every single person."

At the dinner table, Lainey leaned over her plate, remembering at the last second to keep her elbows off the cloth the way the aunties did, and asked the auntie's daughter what the greeting meant. "It means sharing the breath of life," the girl said, passing Hazel the bread basket.

Hazel took a roll, looked down the long table at all those people who had shared their breath with her, and decided she would practise on Lainey the moment they got outside.

"Deal," said Lainey.

activity: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
knowledge_domain: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
fact: In a parallel circuit, each bulb has its own path to the battery, so the others stay lit if one bulb breaks.
story:
The bulb in the middle of the board flickered twice and went dark, which was a problem, because the science fair demonstrations started in twenty minutes and Emily's circuit was supposed to be the centerpiece of her table. Duke poked the dead bulb with a pencil. "Maybe it just needs encouragement."

"It needs a new bulb, and we don't have one," Emily said. She checked the drawer of Mr. Do's lab, where the good supplies lived, but it was locked. Mr. Do had gone to judge another classroom and would not be back before the fair began. There were bulbs in the cabinet across the room, but those were labeled obsolete, which meant, as far as anyone could tell, that half of them worked and nobody wanted to count which half. Duke suggested they quantify it, test every bulb, and Emily pointed out that even if they spent all twenty minutes doing that, the fair would be over.

Abel arrived with a bag of chips and no ideas. "Why is it called a series circuit anyway?" he asked, chewing. Emily started to answer, then stopped, because she was looking at the wire that ran from bulb to bulb to bulb, one single path, like a hallway with three doors. When the middle bulb died, the hallway was blocked. Nothing could get through to the third bulb, which was why it sat dark even though it was probably fine. She couldn't see the electricity, but she could see the wire, and the wire only offered one road.

"Cut it," she said. Abel looked at her. "The wire. Between the first bulb and the last one. Then run a new piece straight from the battery to the last bulb." She drew it on a napkin: two separate roads out of the battery, one for each bulb. Duke, who was better with the wire strippers, cut and connected while Emily held everything steady and Abel supplied commentary, some of it useful. The timer on the wall showed nine minutes when they taped the last joint.

At the table, with parents drifting past, Emily closed the switch. Both bulbs lit, bright and steady. She unscrewed the dead middle bulb completely, so there was clearly nothing but a gap where it had been, and the third bulb stayed on. A woman with a clipboard stopped to watch. "It's a parallel circuit," Emily said. "Each bulb has its own path to the battery, so if one bulb breaks, the others stay lit."

The woman wrote something down. Behind her, Abel held up the dead bulb like a small trophy, and the good bulb burned on without it.
